newsitem.title: POLAND: POLISH FORMER PRIVATISATION MINISTER TO FACE TRIAL.
newsitem.headline: POLISH FORMER PRIVATISATION MINISTER TO FACE TRIAL.

text.p: Prosecutors have charged Poland's liberal former privatisation minister Janusz Lewandowski over alleged irregularities during the sale of two firms in the early 1990s, their spokeswoman said on Monday.

"The charges concern sales of (trading company) Krakchemia and (construction firm) Techma," said Malgorzata Wilkosz-Sliwa from the prosecutors' office in the southern city of Krakow, where the two enterprises are based.

She told Reuters that Lewandowski had allegedly chosen unfavourable offers for stakes in the two companies, which brought losses of 2.4 million zlotys ($827,000 at current rates) to the treasury. If convicted, he could face up to 10 years in prison, she added.
Lewandowski, a champion of Poland's switch from pre-1989 communism to the market economy, firmly denied any wrongdoing.
"The allegations are false. I affirm, and this can be checked in the prosecutors' documents, that there were no better offers," he told Reuters by telephone.

Lewandowski, who won international praise for launching Poland's mass privatisation programme, suggested the allegations might have been designed to disredit him and his opposition party ahead of this year's parliamentary elections.

"I think something very unhealthy is taking place at the prosecutors' office... I think there has been an interest in making the indictment surface during the election year," he said without elaborating.

Lewandowski's Union for Freedom (UW) party is one of several right-wing and centrist groups challenging the two ruling parties, both rooted in the communist system, at the polls. The current coalition has been in power since 1993.
But Wilkosz-Sliwa said that companies with Austrian and U.S. capital had clearly presented better bids to buy the offered stakes in Techma and Krakchemia, than the final buyers.
In the case of Krakchemia, now listed on the Warsaw Stock Exchange's parallel market, Lewandowski also allegedly broke the law by signing a document with an earlier date, she said.
This allowed some of the firm's shareholders to increase their stakes without bidding in a public tender, she added.

Lewandowski, who pioneered Poland's privatisation in 1991-1993, when the law was often ambiguous, has been a target for repeated attacks from political parties and other groups hostile to privatisation.
Until now prosecutors have rejected such complaints. -- Marcin Grajewski +48 22 653 9700
